entries.lesson_title: System Output from Input and Impulse Response
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the LTI system output by evaluating the continuous-time convolution integral for a given input signal and impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: System Output from Input and Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Identifying the Input, Impulse Response, and Output

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$ and impulse response $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$. Which statement correctly identifies $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and $y(t)$?

choice_blocks.text: $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$, $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, and the output is $x(t)*h(t)$.
$x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, and $y(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The phrase "has input" names $x(t)$, and the phrase "impulse response" names $h(t)$. The output is the unknown system response, so it is named $y(t)$ and written as $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$ before any convolution setup.

prompt_blocks.text: A causal LTI system is driven by $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ and has impulse response $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-4)$. Which statement correctly identifies the input signal, impulse response, and output symbol?

choice_blocks.text: $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, $h(t-\tau)=u(t-\tau)-u(t-\tau-4)$, and $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.
$x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-4)$, and the output is $x(t)h(t)$.
$x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, $h(t)=y(t)$, and the output is $u(t)-u(t-4)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The statement says the system is driven by $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, so that is the input. It says the impulse response is $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-4)$. The output symbol is $y(t)$, and for an LTI system it is written as $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.

sections.section_title: Writing the Output as a Convolution Integral

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-3)$ and impulse response $h(t)=e^{-4t}u(t)$. Write $y(t)$ as a convolution integral before substituting the formulas.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output is the convolution of the input and impulse response. This step only writes the template: use $x(\tau)$, use $h(t-\tau)$, integrate over $\tau$, and do not substitute the given formulas yet.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$. Write the system output as a convolution integral before substituting the signal formulas.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The given expressions identify the input and impulse response, but they are not substituted in this section. The convolution setup reads the input at $\tau$ and the impulse response at $t-\tau$.

sections.lesson_title: System Output from Input and Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Substituting x(tau) and h(t - tau) into the Integral

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$, write the substituted convolution integral for $y(t)$, but do not evaluate it.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Start with the convolution template, then replace $t$ by $\tau$ in the input formula and replace $t$ by $t-\tau$ in the impulse-response formula. The integral is only being set up, not evaluated.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-4)$, write the substituted convolution integral for $y(t)$, but do not evaluate it.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The input factor becomes $x(\tau)=e^{-2\tau}u(\tau)$. The impulse-response factor becomes $h(t-\tau)=u(t-\tau)-u(t-\tau-4)$, and those factors are placed inside the same convolution integral.

sections.lesson_title: System Output from Input and Impulse Response
sections.section_title: Evaluating the Integral for the Output Signal

prompt_blocks.text: For an LTI system with input $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)=u(t)$, the convolution setup on $0<t<1$ is $y(t)=\int_0^t e^{-2\tau}\,d\tau$. Evaluate $y(t)$ on this interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The setup and region are already given, so evaluate the definite integral with respect to $\tau$. An antiderivative of $e^{-2\tau}$ is $-\frac{1}{2}e^{-2\tau}$.

prompt_blocks.text: For an LTI system with input $x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)=u(t)$, the convolution setup on $0<t<1$ is $y(t)=\int_0^t e^{-3\tau}\,d\tau$. Evaluate $y(t)$ on this interval.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Use the stated integral directly and keep the stated region attached to the result. An antiderivative of $e^{-3\tau}$ is $-\frac{1}{3}e^{-3\tau}$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Partition a direct convolution calculation into time regions by tracking how the overlap between x(tau) and h(t - tau) changes as t moves.

sections.section_title: Finding Contact Times Between x(tau) and h(t - tau)

image_slots.image_description: Create a clean tau-axis support diagram for a direct convolution contact-time question. Show the fixed support of x(\tau) as a horizontal interval from \tau=1 to \tau=4, labeled x(\tau) nonzero on [1,4]. Show the moving support of h(t-\tau) as a second horizontal interval on the same tau scale from \tau=t-3 to \tau=t-1, labeled h(t-\tau) nonzero on [t-3,t-1]. Do not show amplitudes, integral evaluation, region classification, or solved contact-time values.

Show the fixed support of x(\tau) as a horizontal interval from \tau=-1 to \tau=2, labeled x(\tau) nonzero on [-1,2]. Show the moving support of h(t-\tau) as a second horizontal interval on the same tau scale from \tau=t-5/2 to \tau=t-1/2, labeled h(t-\tau) nonzero on [t-5/2,t-1/2]. prompt_blocks.text: For $x(\tau)$ nonzero on $1\le \tau\le 4$ and $h(t-\tau)$ nonzero on $t-3\le \tau\le t-1$, find the contact times between their support endpoints.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The fixed endpoints are $1$ and $4$. The moving endpoints are $t-3$ and $t-1$, so set each moving endpoint equal to each fixed endpoint.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} t-3=1&\Rightarrow t=4 \\ t-3=4&\Rightarrow t=7 \\ t-1=1&\Rightarrow t=2 \\ t-1=4&\Rightarrow t=5 \end{aligned}

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Sorting those t-values gives the contact times.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(\tau)$ nonzero on $-1\le \tau\le 2$ and $h(t-\tau)$ nonzero on $t-\frac{5}{2}\le \tau\le t-\frac{1}{2}$, find the contact times between their support endpoints.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The fixed endpoints are $-1$ and $2$. The moving endpoints are $t-5/2$ and $t-1/2$, so set each moving endpoint equal to each fixed endpoint.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: \begin{aligned} t-\frac{5}{2}=-1&\Rightarrow t=\frac{3}{2} \\ t-\frac{5}{2}=2&\Rightarrow t=\frac{9}{2} \\ t-\frac{1}{2}=-1&\Rightarrow t=-\frac{1}{2} \\ t-\frac{1}{2}=2&\Rightarrow t=\frac{5}{2} \end{aligned}

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Sorting those t-values gives the contact times.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(\tau)$ supported on $[0,4]$ and $h(t-\tau)$ supported on $[t-2,t]$, give the $\tau$ integration bounds for each overlap region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The $\tau$ bounds come from the intersection of the fixed support and the moving support. The lower bound is the larger left endpoint, and the upper bound is the smaller right endpoint.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the convolution of finite-duration input and impulse-response signals by finding overlap intervals, setting integration bounds, and assembling the piecewise LTI output.

sections.section_title: Finding the Output Support from Finite-Duration Signal Supports

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero only on $-1\le t\le 2$ and $h(t)$ is nonzero only on $0\le t\le 3$, find the possible nonzero support of $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Add the left endpoints to get the first possible nonzero output time, and add the right endpoints to get the last possible nonzero output time.
So the convolution output can be nonzero only on $[-1,5]$.

prompt_blocks.text: If $x(t)$ is nonzero only on $2\le t\le 5$ and $h(t)$ is nonzero only on $-4\le t\le -1$, find the possible nonzero support of $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The outer support interval comes from endpoint sums: earliest with earliest, and latest with latest.
Therefore, the possible nonzero support of $y(t)$ is $[-2,4]$.

sections.section_title: Setting Integral Bounds in a Partial-Overlap Region

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 4$ and $h(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 1$, with both signals zero otherwise. For $0<t<1$, set the $\tau$ integration bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The factor $x(\tau)$ is nonzero on the fixed interval $0\le\tau\le 4$. The factor $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero when $0\le t-\tau\le 1$.
For $0<t<1$, the overlap of $[0,4]$ and $[t-1,t]$ is $[0,t]$, so the bounds are $0\le\tau\le t$.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=2$ on $1\le t\le 5$ and $h(t)=3$ on $0\le t\le 2$, with both signals zero otherwise. For $1<t<3$, set the $\tau$ integration bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitudes do not affect the bounds. The support of $x(\tau)$ is $1\le\tau\le 5$, and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero when $0\le t-\tau\le 2$.
For $1<t<3$, the overlap of $[1,5]$ and $[t-2,t]$ is $[1,t]$, so the $\tau$ bounds are $1\le\tau\le t$.

sections.section_title: Setting Integral Bounds in a Full-Overlap Region

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 5$ and $h(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 2$, with both signals zero otherwise. For $2<t<5$, set the $\tau$ integration bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The support of $x(\tau)$ is the fixed interval $[0,5]$. The support of $h(t-\tau)$ comes from $0\le t-\tau\le 2$.
For $2<t<5$, the moving interval $[t-2,t]$ lies inside $[0,5]$, so the full-overlap bounds are $t-2\le\tau\le t$.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=2$ on $1\le t\le 7$ and $h(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 3$, with both signals zero otherwise. For $4<t<7$, set the $\tau$ integration bounds for $y(t)=\int x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The amplitude of $x(t)$ does not affect the bounds. The fixed support is $1\le\tau\le 7$, and the shifted support of $h(t-\tau)$ is found from $0\le t-\tau\le 3$.
For $4<t<7$, $t-3>1$ and $t<7$, so the moving interval is fully inside the fixed interval. The bounds are $t-3\le\tau\le t$.

sections.section_title: Evaluating Finite-Duration Convolution Pieces

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=3$ on $0\le t\le 4$ and $h(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 1$, with both signals zero otherwise, evaluate $y(t)$ on the regions $0<t<1$ with bounds $0\le\tau\le t$ and $1<t<4$ with bounds $t-1\le\tau\le t$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: On the stated overlap regions, the integrand is constant because $x(\tau)=3$ and $h(t-\tau)=1$.

prompt_blocks.text: For $x(t)=2$ on $0\le t\le 5$ and $h(t)=4$ on $0\le t\le 2$, with both signals zero otherwise, evaluate $y(t)$ on the regions $0<t<2$ with bounds $0\le\tau\le t$ and $2<t<5$ with bounds $t-2\le\tau\le t$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The supplied bounds already restrict the integral to overlap regions. Inside each integral, $x(\tau)=2$ and $h(t-\tau)=4$.

sections.section_title: Assembling the Piecewise Finite-Duration Output

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 4$ and $h(t)=3$ on $0\le t\le 1$, with both signals zero otherwise. Compute and assemble the full piecewise output $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The output support is $[0,5]$. On every nonzero overlap region, the integrand is $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)=1\cdot 3=3$.
The overlap length is $t$ on $0<t<1$, $1$ on $1\le t\le 4$, and $5-t$ on $4<t<5$.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(t)=2$ on $0\le t\le 5$ and $h(t)=1$ on $0\le t\le 2$, with both signals zero otherwise. Compute and assemble the full piecewise output $y(t)=(x*h)(t)$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The possible output support is $[0,7]$. On the nonzero regions, the integrand is constant: $x(\tau)h(t-\tau)=2\cdot 1=2$.
The overlap length is $t$ on $0<t<2$, $2$ on $2\le t\le 5$, and $7-t$ on $5<t<7$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Evaluate direct convolution involving sloped signal segments by expressing the overlapping pieces in tau, setting time-dependent bounds, and integrating the resulting products.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Intersect the fixed support [0,2] with the moving support [t - 1,t]. In this time region, $t - 1 \ge 0$ and $t \le 2$, so the moving interval supplies both overlap endpoints.

prompt_blocks.text: Let $x(\tau)$ be nonzero on $0 \le \tau \le 2$, and let $h(t - \tau)$ be nonzero on $t - 1 \le \tau \le t$. For $2 \le t \le 3$, set the $\tau$-bounds for their overlap.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: Intersect the fixed support [0,2] with the moving support [t - 1,t]. In this time region, $t - 1 \ge 0$, so the lower bound is t - 1. Also $t \ge 2$, so the smaller upper endpoint is 2.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $0 \le t \le 1$, the overlap is $0 \le \tau \le t$. Multiply the sloped factor by the constant factor, then integrate with respect to $\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $2 \le t \le 3$, the overlap is $t - 1 \le \tau \le 2$. Use those overlap bounds, not the full fixed support, and integrate with respect to $\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $0 \le t \le 1$, the overlap is $0 \le \tau \le t$. Multiply the two linear factors before integrating with respect to $\tau$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For $0 \le t \le 1$, the overlap is $0 \le \tau \le t$. The shifted $h(t - \tau)$ factor still depends on $\tau$, so expand the product before integrating.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a rectangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shaded product region is a rectangle, so multiply its $\tau$-width by its constant product height. The $\tau$-width is 2 - t and the height is 2.

prompt_blocks.text: For the shown overlap region, the product $x(\tau)$$h(t - \tau)$ is a right triangle. Use geometry to find the convolution contribution for this region.

entries.lesson_title: Checking Continuity of a Convolution Result
entries.lesson_core_move: Verify a piecewise convolution result by comparing left- and right-hand boundary values at adjacent time regions to catch algebra or region errors.

sections.lesson_title: Checking Continuity of a Convolution Result
sections.section_title: Checking Continuity at a Zero-to-Nonzero Boundary

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise convolution result
which statement correctly checks continuity at $t=2$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_left(2)=0$ and $y_right(5)=3$$(5-2)=9$, so the check fails.
$y_left(2)=0$ and $y_right(2)=3$$(2-2)=0$, so the check passes.
$y_left(2)=0$ and $y_right(2)=0$, but the check fails because the formula changes at $t=2$.
The interval $2 \le t < 5$ has length 3, so the continuity check passes.
The right-hand formula gives $y_right(2)=3$$(2+2)=12$, so the check fails.

questions.correct_answer: $y_left(2)=0$ and $y_right(2)=3$$(2-2)=0$, so the continuity check passes at $t=2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At a zero-to-nonzero boundary, compare the zero piece with the first nonzero formula at the shared boundary time. The left value is 0, and substituting $t=2$ into 3(t-2) also gives 0, so the values match.

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise convolution result
which statement correctly checks continuity at $t=-1$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_left(-1)=0$ and $y_right(-1)=4$$(-1+1)=0$, so the check passes.
$y_left(-1)=0$ and $y_right(2)=4$$(2+1)=12$, so the check fails.
The slope changes from 0 to 4 at $t=-1$, so the continuity check fails.
$y_right(-1)=4$$(-1-1)=-8$, so the check fails.
The nonzero region starts at $t=-1$, so the result is automatically discontinuous there.

questions.correct_answer: $y_left(-1)=0$ and $y_right(-1)=4$$(-1+1)=0$, so the continuity check passes at $t=-1$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared boundary is $t=-1$, so both adjacent pieces must be checked at $t=-1$. The zero side gives 0, and the first nonzero formula gives 4(-1+1)=0, so the boundary values agree.

sections.lesson_title: Checking Continuity of a Convolution Result
sections.section_title: Checking an Interior Boundary Between Two Nonzero Pieces

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise result below, which statement correctly checks continuity at $t = 3$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_left(3)=3-1=2$ and $y_right(3)=5-3=2$, so the check passes.
$y_left(1)=1-1=0$ and $y_right(3)=5-3=2$, so the check fails.
The slopes are 1 and -1, so the check fails.
$y_left(3)=2$ and $y_right(3)=5+3=8$, so the check fails.
The formulas t-1 and 5-t are different, so the result is discontinuous at $t = 3$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At an interior boundary, evaluate both adjacent formulas at the same boundary value. Here the left formula gives 2 and the right formula also gives 2, so the boundary values match and the continuity check passes.

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise result below, which statement correctly checks continuity at $t = 2$?

choice_blocks.text: $y_left(2)=2$$(2)=4$ and $y_right(2)=7-2=5$, so the check fails.
$y_left(0)=2$$(0)=0$ and $y_right(2)=7-2=5$, so the check fails.
$y_left(2)=4$ and $y_right(2)=7+2=9$, so the check fails.
Only the right formula needs to be checked: $y_right(2)=7-2=5$, so the result is continuous.
The slopes are 2 and -1, so the check fails without evaluating the boundary values.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared boundary is $t = 2$, so both adjacent formulas must be evaluated at $t = 2$. The left value is 4 and the right value is 5, so the boundary values do not match and the continuity check fails.

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise result below, which summary correctly checks continuity at every time-region boundary?

$t = 1$: $0 = 0$; $t = 2$: 2 and 2(3+2)=10; $t = 3$: $0 = 0$. Since $t = 2$ fails, not all checks pass.
$t = 2$: 2(2-1)=2 and 2(3-2)=2, so all checks pass.
Compare $y_left(1)=0$ with $y_right(3)=0$; since those endpoint values match, all checks pass.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared boundaries are $t = 1$, $t = 2$, and $t = 3$. At each boundary, the formula immediately to the left and the formula immediately to the right give the same value, so the piecewise result passes all continuity checks.

prompt_blocks.text: For the piecewise result below, which summary correctly checks continuity at every time-region boundary?

$t = 2$: $0 = 0$; at the middle region, compare $y_left(2)=0$ with $y_right(5)=0$; $t = 5$: $0 = 0$. All checks pass.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shared boundaries are $t = 2$, $t = 3$, and $t = 5$. The outer boundary values match, but at $t = 3$ the adjacent formulas give 1 and 2, so the full set of continuity checks does not pass.

sections.lesson_title: Checking Continuity of a Convolution Result
sections.section_title: Using a Failed Continuity Check to Find an Error

prompt_blocks.text: A computed convolution result is shown below. Which boundary check best identifies where the likely error is?

choice_blocks.text: At $t = 1$, the values are 0 and 2(1-1)=0, so recheck the pieces adjacent to $t = 1$.
At $t = 2$, the values are 2(2-1)=2 and $3-2=1$, so recheck the pieces adjacent to $t = 2$.
At $t = 3$, the values are $3-3=0$ and 0, so recheck the final zero region.
Every nonzero piece is linear, so the computed result is continuous.
The slopes 2 and -1 are different at $t = 2$, so replace 3-t with 4-t.

questions.correct_answer: At $t = 2$, the values are 2(2-1)=2 and $3-2=1$, so recheck the pieces adjacent to $t = 2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The boundary $t = 1$ passes and the boundary $t = 3$ passes, but the adjacent formulas at $t = 2$ give different values. That flags the two pieces touching $t = 2$, or the transition between them, as the likely place to investigate.

prompt_blocks.text: A computed convolution result is shown below. Which boundary check best identifies where the likely error is?

choice_blocks.text: At $t = 3$, the values are $3-1=2$ and $5-3=2$, so recheck the pieces adjacent to $t = 3$.
At $t = 2$, the values are 0 and $2-1=1$, so recheck the final zero region $t \ge 5$.
At $t = 2$, the values are 0 and $2-1=1$, so recheck the zero-to-first-nonzero transition at $t = 2$.
The first nonzero interval has width 1 and the second has width 2, so the likely error is in the second nonzero region.
At $t = 2$, the values are 0 and 1, so the corrected first nonzero formula must be t-2.

questions.correct_answer: At $t = 2$, the values are 0 and $2-1=1$, so recheck the zero-to-first-nonzero transition at $t = 2$.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The first shared boundary already fails: the zero piece gives 0 at $t = 2$, while the first nonzero formula gives 1. The continuity check points to the pieces adjacent to $t = 2$, but it does not by itself prove the corrected formula.

sections.lesson_title: Interpreting Convolution as LTI System Output

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and the computed convolution shown below. Which statement correctly identifies the output $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output equals the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Since the computed convolution is $p(t)$, the output is $y(t)=p(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: An LTI system has input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and the computed convolution shown below. Which statement correctly identifies the output $y(t)$?

answer_explanation_blocks.text: For an LTI system, the output is the convolution result. The convolution may be written as h*x or x*h.
Since the computed convolution is $r(t)$, the output is $y(t)=r(t)$.

prompt_blocks.text: The diagram shows a piecewise convolution output with breakpoints $p<q<r$. Which overlap change explains the breakpoint at $t=q$?

Only the height of $h(t-\tau)$ changes; the support overlap stays the same.

questions.correct_answer: The supports reach maximum alignment at $t=q$, so the overlap changes from growing to shrinking.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: A breakpoint marks a support event in the convolution overlap. At $t=q$, the supports are aligned at maximum overlap, so after q the overlap no longer grows in the same way.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: At the last breakpoint, the moving support has reached its final contact with the fixed support. After that point, the two supports no longer overlap, so the output returns to zero.

prompt_blocks.text: Given the plots of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and the resulting $y(t)$, which explanation best accounts for why $y(t)$ rises, levels off, and then falls?

choice_blocks.text: The output has that shape because $x(t)$ is wide; $h(t)$ does not affect the rise, level part, or fall.
The overlap between $x(\tau)$ and $h(t-\tau)$ increases, then stays constant while the shorter pulse is fully inside the longer one, then decreases.
The output has that shape because $h(t)$ is short; $x(t)$ only sets the final endpoint.
The overlap first decreases, then stays constant, then increases, so $y(t)$ falls, levels off, and rises.
The plateau appears because endpoints are labeled b and c, even though the amount of overlap is still changing there.

questions.correct_answer: The output rises as overlap increases, stays level while the overlap amount is constant, and falls as overlap decreases.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: The shape of $y(t)$ comes from the joint overlap in the convolution integral, not from either signal alone. More overlap gives the rising segment, constant full overlap gives the level segment, and shrinking overlap gives the falling segment.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: a<t<b:\ \text{overlap increases},\quad b<t<c:\ \text{overlap is constant},\quad c<t<d:\ \text{overlap decreases}

prompt_blocks.text: Given the plots of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and the resulting $y(t)$, which explanation best accounts for why $y(t)$ rises to a peak and then falls?

choice_blocks.text: The output follows the triangular input $x(t)$ alone; $h(t)$ only changes the height scale.
Because $h(t)$ is rectangular, $y(t)$ must stay level throughout the entire nonzero interval.
The overlap decreases first and then increases, so the output falls before it rises.
As $h(t-\tau)$ overlaps larger values of $x(\tau)$, the weighted overlap grows; after it moves past the largest part of $x(\tau)$, the weighted overlap shrinks.
The labels a, b, and c explain the shape by themselves; the amount or weight of overlap does not matter.

questions.correct_answer: The output rises while the weighted overlap with larger values of $x(\tau)$ grows, then falls after that weighted overlap shrinks.

answer_explanation_blocks.text: With a triangular input, the output shape depends on weighted overlap, not just the presence of any overlap. The value of $y(t)$ grows while the shifted impulse response overlaps larger portions of $x(\tau)$, then decreases after the overlap shifts away from the peak.

answer_explanation_blocks.latex: a<t<b:\ \text{weighted overlap increases},\qquad b<t<c:\ \text{weighted overlap decreases}
